Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Civic life: news, government & the law

debate noun and verb

also a debate, hold a debate, public debate

classical

Cic. Off. 1.34: ūnum per disceptātiōnem, alterum per vim
Traupman 179, 301

disceptātiō, disceptātiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a debate, the arguing out of a disputed point

Lewis & Short: “good prose”, and the word Cicero prefers in his speeches.

Other words

  • disceptō, disceptāre, disceptāvī, disceptātum — debate, argue out (a question)

    verb, first conjugation; dē and the ablative · also used · classical · Liv. 21.19.1: dē foederum jūre verbīs disceptāre; Traupman 177: Dē quō disceptātum est?, What was the debate about?

  • altercātiō, altercātiōnis f. — a sharp exchange of words, as in the senate

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.16.10: redeō ad altercātiōnem; M-O s.v. debate

    Lewis & Short: “a strife or contest in words … with or without passion”; Cicero uses it in his letters and dialogues for heated exchanges, such as his clash with Clodius in the senate.

Examples

  • nam cum sint duo genera dēcertandī, ūnum per disceptātiōnem, alterum per vim, cumque illud proprium sit hominis, hoc bēluārum, cōnfugiendum est ad posterius, sī ūtī nōn licet superiōre

    for there are two ways of settling a dispute, one by debate and the other by force, and since the first belongs to man and the second to beasts, we may resort to the second only if we cannot use the firstCic. Off. 1.34

See also discuss, argument, argument, speech.
